title: Burgundy Level 2 Comprehensive Assessment Question Bank

questions.question: What is the most important grape variety in the Côte de Nuits?
questions.explanation: The Côte de Nuits produces the world's greatest Pinot Noir. Nearly all of the top red-wine Grands Crus are concentrated here, from Gevrey-Chambertin to Nuits-Saint-Georges.

questions.question: Roughly how many hectares is the Romanée-Conti Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Romanée-Conti is only about 1.8 hectares, producing roughly 5,000-6,000 bottles a year. It is one of Burgundy's rarest and most expensive wines, held as a monopole by DRC.

questions.question: What is the Côte de Beaune globally famous for?
options: Primarily top red wine, white as secondary
Primarily top-tier white wine (Chardonnay), concentrating Montrachet, Meursault, and more
questions.explanation: The Côte de Beaune's greatest glory is its top-tier Chardonnay white wines — Montrachet, Meursault, Corton-Charlemagne, and others — the world's greatest concentration of white wine excellence, while also producing top Pinot Noir such as Pommard and Volnay.

questions.question: In what year was Burgundy's "Climat" concept recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage site?
questions.explanation: Burgundy's Climats (the vineyard-plot cultural landscape) were officially inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015, marking the highest global recognition of the French terroir concept.

questions.question: Which two villages does the Montrachet Grand Cru straddle?
questions.explanation: Le Montrachet straddles the boundary between Puligny-Montrachet (north) and Chassagne-Montrachet (south). Both villages appended "Montrachet" to their names to share in its prestige.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Gevrey-Chambertin have?
questions.explanation: Gevrey-Chambertin has more Grands Crus than any other Burgundy village — 9 in total, including Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, Mazis-Chambertin, and Chapelle-Chambertin.

questions.question: The geological foundation of Burgundy's vineyard soils dates mainly from which era?
questions.explanation: Burgundy's soils derive mainly from Jurassic-era (roughly 180-140 million years ago) limestone and marl deposits. These geological layers give the Côte d'Or vineyards their mineral-rich growing environment and are the geological basis for the region's terroir complexity.

questions.question: Which two Grands Crus does DRC (Domaine de la Romanée-Conti) hold as exclusive monopoles?
questions.explanation: DRC holds Romanée-Conti (1.8 ha) and La Tâche (6.06 ha) as complete monopoles, and also owns partial shares of plots such as Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant.

questions.question: How is a Burgundy Grand Cru typically shown on the label?
options: Just the Grand Cru's name (e.g. "Chambertin") — the name itself is the AOC
The country and region name must be included
Quality is indicated with Roman numerals
questions.explanation: A distinctive feature of Burgundy Grand Cru labels: only the Grand Cru's name needs to appear (e.g. "Chambertin"), with no village name required, because the vineyard name itself constitutes an independent AOC ranked above village level.

questions.question: Among Meursault's most famous Premiers Crus, which is known for the strongest minerality (and has been proposed for Grand Cru promotion)?
questions.explanation: Perrières (meaning "quarry") has extremely thin soil with exposed limestone, making it Meursault's most mineral-driven Premier Cru. It has been proposed for Grand Cru status and is widely considered the Meursault plot closest to Grand Cru quality.

questions.question: What slope aspect suits top vineyards best on the Côte d'Or?
questions.explanation: East- or southeast-facing slopes warm quickly in the morning to boost photosynthesis while receiving a gentler angle of sun in the afternoon, preserving acidity, and they're sheltered by hills to the west — a shared feature of Burgundy's finest Climats.

questions.question: How many owners currently share the Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Clos de Vougeot, about 50 hectares, was auctioned off in fragments after the French Revolution and now has more than 80 owners — leading to enormous quality variation between different producers' bottlings from the same Grand Cru, and the strongest evidence for Burgundy's maxim that "the producer matters more than the plot."

questions.question: What is the designated grape variety for Corton-Charlemagne?
questions.explanation: Corton-Charlemagne is a Chardonnay white-wine Grand Cru — one of the Côte de Beaune's most important white Grands Crus, and Burgundy's grandest northern white-wine style, known for its full minerality and exceptional aging potential.

questions.question: What must a Burgundy Premier Cru label show together?
options: Only the plot name, no village name needed
Village name + plot name + Premier Cru
questions.explanation: The standard format for a Premier Cru label is: village AOC + plot name (Climat) + Premier Cru — for example, "Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses Premier Cru." This lets consumers identify both the village character and the specific plot of origin.

questions.question: Burgundy's most common agricultural risk, spring frost, typically occurs in which months?
questions.explanation: The most dangerous time for spring frost in Burgundy is April-May, after budbreak — once frost strikes, the tender young shoots are killed, and in severe cases yields can drop by over 50%. Both 2016 and 2019 were hit hard by this.

questions.question: Of Chambolle-Musigny's two Grands Crus, which is famous for its "feminine elegance"?
options: Le Musigny (known for its floral elegance)
questions.explanation: Le Musigny is one of Burgundy's most refined and elegant Grands Crus, known for rose and violet aromas and a silky texture. Bonnes-Mares, in the same village, is fuller and more robust by contrast.

questions.question: Comparing the 2015 and 2010 Burgundy vintages, which is generally regarded as fuller-bodied overall?
questions.explanation: 2015 Burgundy is known for exceptionally full fruit and a silky texture (many compare it to 1990); 2010 is known for cool elegance and high acidity — a more "classic" Burgundy style. Both have passionate advocates, but 2015 is the fuller of the two.

questions.question: When assessing tannin quality in Burgundy Pinot Noir, what is the highest praise?
options: Powerful and dense, like Bordeaux Cabernet
Silky and fine, gliding smoothly without scratching the throat
questions.explanation: The benchmark for top Burgundy Pinot Noir tannin is: silky/velvety, gliding smoothly with no coarseness or irritation whatsoever. Excessive astringency signals over-extraction or under-ripeness — a clear quality flaw.

questions.question: Domaine Armand Rousseau is best known for the wines of which village?
questions.explanation: Armand Rousseau is a legendary estate in Gevrey-Chambertin, holding top plots such as Chambertin, Clos de Bèze, and Clos Saint-Jacques. Using traditional whole-cluster fermentation and minimal intervention, it produces some of Burgundy's greatest Chambertin wines.

questions.question: What effect does whole-cluster fermentation have on Pinot Noir?
options: Lowers alcohol, making the wine lighter
The stems contribute tannin and a spicy character, adding structure and complexity
Makes the wine ready to drink sooner
Mainly used to increase color depth
questions.explanation: Whole-cluster fermentation is a traditional Burgundy practice: the stems contribute a different type of tannin (coarser but structuring), a distinctive spice/herbal character, and one of Burgundy's most recognizable "forest floor" aromas. It's an important stylistic tool for top estates.

questions.question: What is the most directly measurable effect of climate warming on Burgundy?
options: The grape variety switched from Pinot Noir to Syrah
Harvest dates have moved about 2 weeks earlier on average over the past 50 years
Climate warming has had no significant effect on Burgundy
questions.explanation: Scientific records show: in the 1980s, Burgundy harvest averaged early October; from the 2010s onward it often begins in late August to early September — about 2 weeks earlier. This systematic shift in harvest timing is the most direct agricultural indicator of climate warming.

questions.question: What effect does "élevage sur lies" (aging on lees) have on Chardonnay's style?
options: Adds roundness, fullness, and toasty/buttery aromas
questions.explanation: Aging on lees: as dead yeast cells break down, they release proteins and polysaccharides, adding creaminess and fullness to the wine and producing its signature toasty, buttery aromas — a key winemaking step for top Meursault and Puligny Chardonnay.

questions.question: What is the single most important indicator of a Burgundy wine's long-term aging potential?
options: The deeper the color, the more it can age
Sufficient natural acidity (the most important anti-oxidation mechanism)
The more oak, the more it can age
The higher the alcohol, the more it can age
questions.explanation: Natural acidity is the single most crucial safeguard for aging: high acidity slows the rate of oxidation, protects fruit character from premature decline, and allows the wine to develop more complex tertiary aromas over time. This is why a lean, high-acid vintage can sometimes outlast a big, low-acid one.

questions.question: Les Amoureuses is one of Burgundy's most famous Premiers Crus. Which village is it in?
questions.explanation: Les Amoureuses ("the lovers") is Chambolle-Musigny's most famous Premier Cru, lying just below the Le Musigny Grand Cru. Its quality approaches Grand Cru level, and its auction prices sometimes surpass certain Grands Crus.

questions.question: What tertiary aromas are typically described in top Burgundy Pinot Noir after 10+ years of aging?
options: Fresh red fruit like strawberry and raspberry
Truffle, leather, forest floor, wild mushroom
questions.explanation: The tertiary (aged) aromas shown by top aged Burgundy Pinot Noir include: truffle (the highest-praised indicator), leather, forest-floor decaying leaves, wild mushroom (porcini, etc.), and black tea — these complex aromas represent the pinnacle achievement of aged Burgundy.

questions.question: Which estate is among Burgundy's most famous representatives of biodynamic viticulture?
questions.explanation: Lalou Bize-Leroy is Burgundy's most famous pioneer of biodynamic viticulture — her Domaine Leroy converted fully in the 1980s. DRC and Domaine Leflaive are also well-known biodynamic estates, but Leroy was the earliest and most radical advocate.

questions.question: Which Burgundy village, though one of the Côte de Nuits' most important, has no Grand Cru at all?
questions.explanation: Nuits-Saint-Georges is the important commercial town at the southern end of the Côte de Nuits, home to many négociants — yet surprisingly it has no Grand Cru. Despite the exceptional quality of Premiers Crus like Les Saint-Georges, historical attempts at promotion have not succeeded.

questions.question: What characterizes Pommard's red-wine style in the Côte de Beaune?
options: Powerful and full, with dense tannin — the Côte de Beaune's most "masculine" Pinot Noir
A light style ready to drink young
questions.explanation: Pommard and Volnay are neighbors with opposite styles: Pommard is robust and full, deep in color with high tannin — the Côte de Beaune red closest to Côte de Nuits power; Volnay, by contrast, is light, often called the most refined "grande dame" among French Pinot Noir.

questions.question: What does "caudalie" mean in wine tasting?
options: A unit measuring finish length (1 caudalie = 1 second)
A way of measuring alcohol content
The proportion of oak barrel used
questions.explanation: Caudalie is a French tasting term specifically for finish length, where 1 caudalie = 1 second. Top Burgundy Grand Cru finishes typically exceed 30 caudalies, and legendary vintages from producers like DRC can exceed 60 — one of the most direct quantitative indicators of quality.

questions.question: What is Domaine Coche-Dury most famous for?
options: Top Pinot Noir from the Côte de Nuits
questions.explanation: Domaine Coche-Dury, founded by Jean-François Coche-Dury (now run by his son Raphaël), is considered one of the greatest achievements in Meursault — and Chardonnay globally. Its Corton-Charlemagne and top Premiers Crus are produced in tiny quantities, with secondary-market prices rivaling DRC's reds.

questions.question: In the Level 2 course, which slope aspect is most favorable for growing Grand Cru grapes?
options: Southeast-facing (full morning sun, gentler afternoon light)
questions.explanation: Southeast- (or east-) facing slopes are the ideal aspect for Côte d'Or vineyards: rapid morning warming speeds up photosynthesis, while the lower afternoon sun angle avoids overheating; the slopes are also sheltered from harsh Atlantic winds from the west — favoring balanced ripening for both Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
